results.q: What happens when the output buffer is full while encoding?
answer: When the output buffer is full while encoding, `pb_write()` checks `stream->bytes_written + count < stream->bytes_written || stream->bytes_written + count > stream->max_size` and then evaluates `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "stream full")`. This causes the function to return immediately with a "stream full" error.

This is handled in pb_write() (pb_encode.c:95): it checks `count > 0 && stream->callback != NULL`, and when that is true it checks `stream->bytes_written + count < stream->bytes_written || stream->bytes_written + count > stream->max_size` (line 97); then it evaluates `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "stream full")` (line 100); then it returns (line 100); then it checks `!stream->callback(stream, buf, count)` (line 107); then it calls one of write_callback(), buf_write() through pb_ostream_s.callback — which one depends on the data at run time (line 107); then it evaluates `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "io error")` (line 108).

buf_write() sets `pb_byte_t *dest = (pb_byte_t*)stream->state` (line 55); then it sets `stream->state = dest + count` (line 56); then it checks `buf != NULL` (line 64); if true it calls memcpy(); then it returns `true` (line 69).

results.q: What happens when the decoder needs more bytes than are left in the input?
answer: When the decoder needs more bytes than are left, `pb_read()` checks `stream->bytes_left < count`; if true it records an error with `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")`. The caller `pb_skip_varint()` then sees `!pb_read(stream, &byte, 1)` and returns `false`.
This is handled in pb_read() (pb_decode.c:103): it checks `stream->bytes_left < count`, and when that is true it records it (`PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")`).
When it does not return there, pb_read() goes on to call read_callback() with (`stream`, `buf`, `count`) (line 107); buf_read() with (`stream`, `buf`, `count`) (line 107).
Its caller pb_skip_varint() checks `!pb_read(stream, &byte, 1)` (pb_decode.c:261) and then returns `false`.

results.q: What happens when a decoded message is missing a required field?
answer: When a required field is missing, the decoder detects the problem in `decode_static_field()` and sets an error. It then returns `false`, skipping the rest of the field processing (no `memset()`, no `pb_field_iter_begin()`, and no further decoding).
Losing the data is detected in decode_static_field() (pb_decode.c:510), which checks `wire_type == PB_WT_STRING && PB_LTYPE(field->type) <= PB_LTYPE_LAST_PACKABLE` (PB_WT_STRING = 2).

When that happens it sets `field->pData = (char*)field->pField + field->data_size * (*size)`; sets `field->pData = (char*)field->pData + field->data_size`; sets `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "array overflow")`; calls pb_make_string_substream() (which checks `!pb_decode_varint32(stream, &size)` (line 389); if true it returns `false` straight away, sets `*substream = *stream` (line 392), checks `substream->bytes_left < size` (line 393)); calls decode_basic_field() (which chooses a case based on `PB_LTYPE(field->type)` (line 428), checks `wire_type != PB_WT_VARINT && wire_type != PB_WT_PACKED` (PB_WT_VARINT = 0, PB_WT_PACKED = 255) (line 431), evaluates `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "wrong wire type")` (line 432)); calls pb_close_string_substream() (which checks `substream->bytes_left` (line 409), checks `!pb_read(substream, NULL, substream->bytes_left)` (line 410); if true it returns `false` straight away, updates stream (state, errmsg; lines 414–417)); returns, so decode_basic_field(), memset(), pb_field_iter_begin() no longer run.

Note that this only triggers when all of these hold: `wire_type == PB_WT_STRING`; `PB_LTYPE(field->type) <= PB_LTYPE_LAST_PACKABLE`. For example, when `wire_type == PB_WT_STRING` is false this path is not taken.

decode_static_field() also stops early when `!pb_make_string_substream(stream, &substream)` (line 519), which skips decode_basic_field(), pb_close_string_substream(); or when `!pb_close_string_substream(stream, &substream)` (line 535), which skips decode_basic_field(), memset(), pb_field_iter_begin() — so without fresh valid data it does not reach those calls either.

results.q: What happens when a varint is too long?
answer: When a varint exceeds the maximum length, `pb_decode_varint()` records an error with `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "varint overflow")`. The caller `pb_decode_svarint()` then returns `false`, and its caller `pb_dec_varint()` also returns `false`.
This is handled in pb_decode_varint() (pb_decode.c:244): it checks `bitpos >= 63 && (byte & 0xFE) != 0`, and when that is true it records it (`PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "varint overflow")`).
Its caller pb_decode_svarint() checks `!pb_decode_varint(stream, &value)` (pb_decode.c:1415) and then returns `false`.
Its caller pb_dec_varint() checks `!pb_decode_svarint(stream, &svalue)` (pb_decode.c:1514) and then returns `false`.

results.q: What happens when a field arrives with the wrong wire type?
answer: When a field arrives with a wrong wire type, `decode_basic_field()` records an error via `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "wrong wire type")`. If the check passes, the function then attempts to decode the field using the appropriate decoder (`pb_dec_bool()`, `pb_dec_varint()`, `pb_decode_fixed32()`, `pb_decode_fixed64()`, or `pb_dec_bytes()`). Other parts of the code also reject bad input, such as `decode_callback_field()`, `decode_static_field()`, and `pb_decode_inner()` rejecting the field when the wire type is inappropriate.

Invalid data is caught in decode_basic_field() (pb_decode.c:431): it checks `wire_type != PB_WT_VARINT && wire_type != PB_WT_PACKED`, and when that is true it records it (`PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "wrong wire type")`).

When it does not return there, decode_basic_field() goes on to call pb_dec_bool() with (`stream`, `field`) (line 434); pb_dec_varint() with (`stream`, `field`) (line 442); pb_decode_fixed32() with (`stream`, `field->pData`) (line 448); pb_decode_fixed64() with (`stream`, `field->pData`) (line 464); pb_dec_bytes() with (`stream`, `field`) (line 471).

Bad input is also rejected in other places: decode_callback_field() rejects it when `wire_type == PB_WT_STRING` (pb_decode.c:799), reporting `*(pb_size_t*)field->pSize = field->tag`; decode_static_field() rejects it when `wire_type == PB_WT_STRING && PB_LTYPE(field->type) <= PB_LTYPE_LAST_PACKABLE` (pb_decode.c:510); pb_decode_inner() rejects it when `!pb_skip_field(stream, wire_type)` (pb_decode.c:1133).

results.q: What happens when messages are nested too deeply?
answer: When a message is nested too deeply, `decode_static_field()` attempts to set defaults for the sub‑message via `pb_message_set_to_defaults()`. If that call fails, it returns the error "failed to set defaults" and stops decoding the nested message.

This is handled in decode_static_field() (pb_decode.c:571): it checks `pb_field_iter_begin(&submsg_iter, field->submsg_desc, field->pData)`, and when that is true it checks `!pb_message_set_to_defaults(&submsg_iter)` (line 573); then it evaluates `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "failed to set defaults")` (line 574); then it returns (line 574).
When it does not return there, decode_static_field() goes on to call decode_basic_field() with (`stream`, `wire_type`, `field`) (line 580).

pb_message_set_to_defaults() sets `pb_wire_type_t wire_type = PB_WT_VARINT` (line 1013); then it checks `iter->descriptor->default_value` (line 1016); if true it calls pb_istream_from_buffer() and sets `defstream = pb_istream_from_buffer(iter->descriptor->default_value, (size_t)-1)`; then it checks `!pb_decode_tag(&defstream, &wire_type, &tag, &eof)` (line 1019); if true it returns `false` straight away; then it repeats while `pb_field_iter_next(iter)` (line 1023); then it checks `!pb_field_set_to_default(iter)` (line 1025); if true it returns `false` straight away; then it checks `tag != 0 && iter->tag == tag` (line 1028).

results.q: What happens when an array has more items than its maximum size during encoding?
answer: When `encode_array()` sees that the array count exceeds the declared maximum size, it records an error by calling `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "array max size exceeded")` and stops further processing.

This is handled in encode_array() (pb_encode.c:150): it checks `PB_ATYPE(field->type) != PB_ATYPE_POINTER && count > field->array_size`, and when that is true it records it (`PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "array max size exceeded")`).

When it does not return there, encode_array() goes on to call pb_encode_tag() with (`stream`, `PB_WT_STRING`, `field->tag`) (line 157); pb_enc_varint() with (`&sizestream`, `field`) (line 175); pb_encode_varint() with (`stream`, `(pb_uint64_t)size`) (line 183); pb_write() with (`stream`, `NULL`, `size`) (line 187); pb_enc_fixed() with (`stream`, `field`) (line 194).

results.q: What happens when the decoder reads a tag of zero?
answer: When the decoder reads a tag of zero, it triggers an error: it calls `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "zero tag")` and returns immediately.

This is handled in pb_decode_inner() (pb_decode.c:1088): it checks `tag == 0`, and when that is true it checks `flags & PB_DECODE_NULLTERMINATED` (line 1090); then it evaluates `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "zero tag")` (line 1097); then it returns (line 1097).

When it does not return there, pb_decode_inner() goes on to call pb_field_iter_find() with (`&iter`, `tag`) (line 1101); pb_field_iter_find_extension() with (`&iter`) (line 1106); decode_extension() with (`stream`, `tag`, `wire_type`) (line 1122); pb_skip_field() with (`stream`, `wire_type`) (line 1133); decode_field() with (`stream`, `wire_type`, `&iter`) (line 1169).

It is called by pb_read() at pb_decode.c:93, only when `count == 0` is false, only when `buf == NULL && stream->callback != buf_read` is true, repeatedly inside `while (count > 16)`; pb_read() at pb_decode.c:99, only when `count == 0` is false, only when `buf == NULL && stream->callback != buf_read` is true; pb_skip_varint() at pb_decode.c:261, repeatedly inside `do-while`; pb_skip_string() at pb_decode.c:278, only when `!pb_decode_varint32(stream, &length)` is false, only when `(size_t)length != length` is false. It is also called by pb_skip_field() (pb_decode.c:326), pb_skip_field() (pb_decode.c:328), read_raw_value() (pb_decode.c:354), read_raw_value() (pb_decode.c:361), read_raw_value() (pb_decode.c:365), pb_close_string_substream() (pb_decode.c:410), pb_decode_fixed32() (pb_decode.c:1433), pb_decode_fixed64() (pb_decode.c:1456), pb_dec_bytes() (pb_decode.c:1590), pb_dec_string() (pb_decode.c:1632), pb_dec_fixed_length_bytes() (pb_decode.c:1715). The full chain from the program's start is: main() → listdir() → pb_decode_ex() → pb_close_string_substream() → pb_read().

`pb_ostream_s.bytes_written` is set by `pb_ostream_from_buffer()` (line 86), by `pb_write()` (line 112), and by `pb_encode_submessage()` (lines 768 and 775). It is read by `main()` (line 32), `pb_write()` (line 97), `encode_array()` (line 180), `pb_get_encoded_size()` (line 573), and `pb_encode_submessage()` (line 750). The value flows from `pb_ostream_s.bytes_written` through `pb_encode_submessage()` → `pb_write()` → `write_callback()` → `send()` and ultimately influences the socket send.
pb_ostream_s.bytes_written is a field of type `size_t`, defined in pb_encode.h:51 — the code describes it as: "Number of bytes written so far.".

It is set by pb_ostream_from_buffer() (`stream.bytes_written = 0`, line 86); pb_write() (`stream->bytes_written += count`, line 112); pb_encode_submessage() (`substream.bytes_written = 0`, line 768); pb_encode_submessage() (`stream->bytes_written += substream.bytes_written`, line 775).
It is read by main() (line 32), pb_write() (line 97), encode_array() (line 180), pb_get_encoded_size() (line 573), pb_encode_submessage() (line 750).
Following where its value goes: pb_ostream_s.bytes_written → pb_encode_submessage() → pb_write() → write_callback() → send() — so it ultimately influences send(), which is an output (socket send).

In short: pb_ostream_s.bytes_written carries a value produced by pb_encode_submessage(), pb_ostream_from_buffer(), pb_write() and consumed by encode_array(), main(), pb_encode_submessage(), feeding send(). pb_encode_submessage(), pb_write() both reads and updates it, so it also keeps state between calls.

results.q: Where is the stream error message errmsg set?
answer: The stream’s `errmsg` field is set in `pb_encode_submessage()` (pb_encode.c:745 and pb_encode.c:778) by assigning `stream->errmsg = substream.errmsg`. It is also cleared in `pb_decode_tag()` (pb_decode.c:308).
It is set in pb_message_set_to_defaults():
pb_message_set_to_defaults() (pb_decode.c:1009).

Step by step, it sets `pb_wire_type_t wire_type = PB_WT_VARINT` (line 1013); then it checks `iter->descriptor->default_value` (line 1016); if true it calls pb_istream_from_buffer() and sets `defstream = pb_istream_from_buffer(iter->descriptor->default_value, (size_t)-1)`; then it checks `!pb_decode_tag(&defstream, &wire_type, &tag, &eof)` (line 1019); if true it returns `false` straight away; then it repeats while `pb_field_iter_next(iter)` (line 1023); then it checks `!pb_field_set_to_default(iter)` (line 1025); if true it returns `false` straight away; then it checks `tag != 0 && iter->tag == tag` (line 1028); then it checks `!decode_field(&defstream, wire_type, iter)` (line 1031); if true it returns `false` straight away; then it checks `!pb_decode_tag(&defstream, &wire_type, &tag, &eof)` (line 1033); if true it returns `false` straight away; then it checks `iter->pSize` (line 1036); if true it sets `*(bool*)iter->pSize = false`; then it calls pb_field_iter_next() (line 1039); ….

Related values are also set here: `stream->errmsg = substream.errmsg` in pb_encode_submessage() (pb_encode.c:745); `iter->message = message` in pb_field_iter_begin() (pb_common.c:161); `iter->submessage_index = 0` in advance_iterator() (pb_common.c:131); `iter->submessage_index = (pb_size_t)(iter->submessage_index + PB_LTYPE_IS_SUBMSG(prev_type))` in advance_iterator() (pb_common.c:152); `stream->errmsg = substream.errmsg` in pb_encode_submessage() (pb_encode.c:778); `stream->errmsg = NULL` in pb_decode_tag() (pb_decode.c:308).
The value is computed just before: `pb_type_t prev_type = (prev_descriptor >> 8) & 0xFF` (pb_common.c:143).
